t: Maximum Sum of M Non-Overlapping Subarrays II
o: We must pick between 1 and m disjoint subarrays of nums, each with length in [l, r], maximizing total sum. Subarrays may not overlap, but gaps are free. In Example 1 we take [4,1] and [2] for 7. In Example 4 every subarray is negative, yet we still must take at least one, so the answer is the least-negative single element, -1. With n up to 1e5 and m up to n, an O(n^2)-state DP is too slow if each state scans all lengths naively; prefix sums plus a sliding-window maximum bring the length scan to amortized O(1).
k: Prefix sums turn 'subarray sum ending at i with length len' into P[i]-P[i-len], separating the i-dependent part P[i] from a window quantity.

a.i: Let f[j][i] be the best total using at most j subarrays inside the first i elements, where f[j][0] = -infinity for j >= 1 so the empty selection is forbidden and at least one subarray is always taken. Either we don't end a subarray at i (f[j][i-1]), or the last subarray is nums[i-len..i-1] for some len in [l, r], giving f[j-1][i-len] + P[i] - P[i-len]. Trying every length directly is correct but slow.
s: Fill the DP table for j = 1..m, i = 1..n, scanning all lengths l..r.
a.t: O(n * m * r) time — three nested loops over count, position, and length; O(n) space with two rolling rows.
a.sp: O(n) — two DP rows and the prefix-sum array.

a.n: Approach 2: Sliding-window maximum with a monotonic deque
a.i: Rewrite the transition as f[j][i] = max(f[j][i-1], P[i] + max over t in [i-r, i-l] of (f[j-1][t] - P[t])). As i grows by 1, the window of t slides by 1, so a monotonically decreasing deque gives the window maximum in amortized O(1). This removes the length scan entirely.
s: For each j, sweep i = 1..n maintaining a deque of candidates prev[t] - P[t] with indices in [i-r, i-l].
Take cur[i] = max(cur[i-1], deque front + P[i]); answer is f[m][n].
a.t: O(n * m) time — each index enters and leaves the deque once per layer; O(n) space.
a.sp: O(n) — two DP rows, prefix sums, and the deque.

w: In an interview, present the DP first, then optimize with the deque — the decomposition P[i] + (f[t] - P[t]) is the key move. Pitfalls: totals can exceed 32-bit range (use 64-bit), at least one subarray must be taken even when everything is negative (base f[j][0] = -inf handles this), and l may exceed i early in the sweep. Follow-ups: what if exactly k subarrays were required, or if subarrays had to be adjacent?
